{"answers":[{"question_id":"Q001_histone_related_proteins","answer":"In SCOPe 2.08, the canonical histone relationship is: class a, “All alpha proteins” → fold a.22, “Histone-fold” → superfamily a.22.1, “Histone-fold.” Within that superfamily, SCOPe separates four informative families. (1) Nucleosome core histones, a.22.1.1: H2A, H2B, H3, H4, and the histone domain of macro-H2A.1. Membership in the same family is the strongest classification-level relationship here and is consistent with relatively close divergence/duplication. (2) Archaeal histones, a.22.1.2. (3) The TAF-related family, a.22.1.3: TAF(II)42, TAF(II)62, TAF(II)18, TAF(II)28, the histone-fold domains of TAF(II)-135/130/hTAF4 and TAF(II)-20/15/hTAF12, NC2 alpha and beta, NF-Y beta and gamma, CHRAC-14 and CHRAC-16, and the histone domain of Son of sevenless. (4) Bacterial histone-fold proteins, a.22.1.4, including Aq_328 and TTHA1479. The archaeal, TAF-related, and bacterial families are related to core histones at the superfamily level: SCOPe treats their shared fold as evidence of probable remote common ancestry, but not close family-level equivalence or shared nucleosome function.

The levels must not be conflated. A family assignment is stronger than a superfamily assignment; a shared fold alone establishes structural similarity but need not establish homology; and the all-alpha class is only a broad architectural category with essentially no evolutionary force. In this release, a.22 contains only the a.22.1 superfamily, but that does not make “same fold” generally equivalent to “homologous.” Classification is also domain-specific: TAFs, Son of sevenless, macro-H2A.1, and other multidomain proteins are related to histones only through the classified histone-fold domain, not necessarily over their full lengths.

Several names are potentially misleading. Linker histones H1/H5 are biologically histones, but their globular domains are placed in the separate winged-helix superfamily a.4.5 and family a.4.5.13, not in the histone-fold. Bacterial H-NS “histone-like” proteins occupy the distinct fold/superfamily a.155/a.155.1, so their similarity is functional or nominal rather than an a.22 histone-fold relationship. Likewise, histone-modifying enzymes are substrate-related, not histone homologs; for example, HDACs are classified in the arginase/deacetylase lineage c.42.1.2.

Consequently, nucleosome assembly, DNA-binding mode, oligomerization, or enzymatic function must not be transferred merely from shared superfamily, fold, or class. A structural template should match the particular domain boundary, sequence coverage, oligomeric context, and experimental quality; multidomain portions outside the histone fold require separate templates.
